title: Mindfulness of breathing
hookLine: of all the things to watch, why the breath? one answer from the suttas, and one from a neighbor
tomorrow: what is the peace the whole path is pointing at?

cards: A coach before a free throw, a nurse before a shot, a friend before a hard phone call: take a breath. So, of all the things a person could watch, why the breath? It's always here, wherever you are.
It runs on its own, and it also lets you steer. And it never repeats: this breath isn't the last one. That makes it a teacher you carry everywhere.

teach.h: LONG IS LONG. SHORT IS SHORT.
teach.b: In the Anapanasati Sutta, anapanasati, mindfulness of breathing, begins very small. Breathing in long, know: I breathe in long. Breathing in short, know: short.
Then sense the whole body breathing. Then let the body calm.
That's four steps; the sutta lays out sixteen, in four sets of four, moving from the body to feelings, to the mind, to letting go.
In another sutta the Buddha compares the practice to a rain that comes out of season at the end of the hot months, settling the dust all at once. Now, a neighbor.

teach.h: THE BREATH OF LIFE, IN GENESIS.
teach.b: In Genesis, a book Jews and Christians share, the breath arrives as a gift.
In the King James words: "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul."
Shared ground: both traditions point at the breath as the closest sign of being alive, and both slow down for it.

One honest difference: in Genesis the breath comes from God, and noticing it can turn a person toward the giver. The Buddha's practice doesn't ask where the breath came from. It watches it come, and go, and come again.

how: Mindfulness of breathing is taught across Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana schools; some Theravada teachers follow the sixteen steps of the Anapanasati Sutta, beginning with simply knowing long and short breaths.

o: holding the breath to quiet the mind
slowing the breath to a count of four
knowing each breath as it comes and goes

s: mindfulness of breathing means controlling your breath
the first steps only know it: long breath, long; short breath, short.
the Anapanasati Sutta lays out sixteen steps in four sets of four
starting with knowing long and short breaths, then the whole body, then calming it.
in Genesis, the breath of life is breathed into the first human by God
"breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul."

games.q: your dad is pacing over a parking ticket, breathing hard. he asks how you stay so calm. what's the sutta's first step?
o: breathe in for four, hold for four, out for four, on a count.
know the breath as it is: long is long, short is short.
hold your breath until the anger passes on its own.
games.why: the sutta starts with knowing, not steering: breathing in long, know it's long. calming comes later, as the fourth step.

practice: Close your eyes or lower them, and breathe without steering. When a breath is long, know it's long; when it's short, know it's short. Those are the first two steps of sixteen, and two minutes is a fine place to start.

wordCard.voice: Mindfulness of breathing: knowing each breath as it is, in and out. In Pali, anapanasati. Sixteen steps, and the first is simply knowing.

orig.note: Pali: ana and apana, breathing in and out, with sati, mindfulness.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: the breath again, whenever you lose your place. Twenty-seven of forty.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 118 (Anapanasati Sutta: the sixteen steps, beginning with knowing long and short breaths, experiencing the whole body, calming the bodily formation)
Samyutta Nikaya 54.9 (mindfulness of breathing likened to an out-of-season rain cloud in the last month of the hot season that settles dust at once)
Visuddhimagga 8 (mindfulness of breathing as a meditation subject)
